article_hits.title: Why are we still working this hard?
article_hits.content: Why Are We Still Working This Hard? In 1973, what a forty-hour week of work produced takes sixteen hours to produce today. That’s according to Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) input output tables. An hour of work in American business now makes two and a half times what it made in 1973. For every forty hours that used to be needed, twenty-four have been freed. You have probably not noticed them. The forty-hour week was written into American law by an act of 1938, and hasn’t changed. Counted for each head of population, the hours worked in American business in 2024 were 10 percent higher than in 1973. As a country, the US took the whole of fifty years’ progress as more output and none of it as time. It was supposed to go differently. article_hits.content: Clashes in Barcelona as thousands join Spain general strike Image source, Reuters By Nick Beake , Europe correspondent , Reporting from Madrid , Guy Hedgecoe , Reporting from Madrid and Alba Morgade Published 11 November 2026, 14:06 GMT Updated 24 minutes ago Clashes have broken out between groups of protesters and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas. Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
